doc.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024

title: Teaching himself to arrange from Russo's book and the chart 'So What'
summary: He bought Bill Russo's arranging book, wrote a blues chart called 'So What' for the high school band, and later struggled in theory classes.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Was there a point when you were trying to play along that you started to realize the relationship between the trumpet notes and the background? The chords or the bass line?

When I got into coll — or into high school I started to get more and more curious about some of those things. And I remember going to the Walden Book Store in the mall and I bought Bill Russo’s How to Arrange for Jazz Orchestra. And I actually wrote a chart. And my teacher helped me a little bit, and there was a student teacher there at the time that helped me a little bit, but I didn’t know what I was doing at all, and Russo’s book is not that easy to digest, especially when you don’t know anything, but it showed me the ranges of the instruments and things like that, so I could piece something toget — so I actually wrote a chart that’s — you know very simple, but I was able to then kind of match harmony up to what was going on and the counter lines and everything, I was actually able to start to figure some of that out. And I finished it and we were able to play it. I don’t think we ever played it in public, again, it wasn’t anything that was earth shattering but I taught myself some of that. And then when I got in college though and had to take the music theory classes, I kind of taught myself the wrong way. So it didn’t exactly match up because I kind of had just done this by the piano and figuring out what fit together and sounded right. So when I actually got into music theory classes it was a little, I don’t know it was probably no more difficult than it would have been but it was difficult at first for me.
Can you recall the name of the chart? Was it a chart that something else you were arranging — another tune?

I do. And the funny thing is one of my friends came up with it and it was “So What” but none of us ever heard the actual “So What” at that time. So I think my friend thought it would just be a funny title, like you know so what? And so that was the title of it, and had no idea that it was the title at that point, because apparently I hadn’t run across “Kind of Blue” yet. So you know that was, like I said probably eleventh, twelfth grade I guess.

Yeah. I have a very similar experience. I believe I did “Well I Think I’m Going Out of My Head.” You know for the high school jazz band. And it probably didn’t work very well but there’s nothing like that first time you hear something back that you’ve toiled over, especially with paper and pencil.

That was the only time I ever did it, but it was a great exercise in kind of at least starting to understand things that I didn’t understand before. But hearing it played back was kind of fun. I remember I spent a long time writing a bass line. It was a blues. I mean it was a 12-bar blues. But I wrote out a bass line that I figured out on the piano. And I remember the bass player in the band was just like, “It’s a blues, I don’t want to play that.” And the teacher is like, “No, play what he wrote.” And he’s like, “Well I don’t want to play —” and things like that you know, but you don’t know. And I remember I did not write a drum part because I couldn’t figure that out. I had no idea how to even begin to do that.
I let that go. I didn’t have any interest in that at all.
